title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about the documents that carry research: the literature review, the research proposal and the report. Each is a genre with its own job and its own conventions, and the work here is producing them well. By the end you will be able to explain how a literature review critiques the discourse, shape a proposal as a framework of questions, and structure a report so its core elements do their work.

These genres are where a research project becomes visible to others. A marker, a supervisor or a funding panel reads your review, proposal or report and judges the work through it. Knowing what each genre is for, and writing to that purpose, is what turns sound research into work that is recognised and trusted.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how a literature review critiques the discourse rather than describing it
shape a research proposal as a framework of questions that makes a project's freshness clear
structure a research report so its core elements do their work for the reader.

title: In real academic practice
body: These genres are the working documents of research in every discipline. A literature review opens a dissertation or an article; a proposal wins approval or funding for a project; a report communicates what was done and what was found. Produce them well now and you are equipped for the research your degree, and much professional work, will ask of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons, one per genre. First, the literature review: how it critiques the discourse rather than listing who said what. Second, the research proposal: how a framework of questions narrows a topic and shows its freshness. Third, the report: how its core elements are organised, and why results and discussion stay apart. Work through them in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can explain how a literature review critiques the discourse rather than describing it.
I can shape a research proposal as a framework of questions that makes a project's freshness clear.
I can structure a research report so its core elements do their work for the reader.

title: Orientation
body: You have read literature reviews, and you may have been asked to write one. It is easy to produce a competent-looking review that is really just a list: this author found this, that author reported that. This lesson is about the difference between that list and a genuine review, which critiques the literature rather than reporting it.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You already read sources critically and know what a literature review is for. The step here is to produce one: to turn your reading into a review that analyses, evaluates and synthesises the discourse, and makes the case for your own research as it goes.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that a literature review critiques the discourse rather than describing who said what
recognise analysis, evaluation and synthesis at work in a worked literature review
identify a sentence that reviews the literature rather than merely listing it in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A literature review provides a review of the literature relevant to your research. It establishes the key works and authors, the important themes, the live debates and the controversial points, what is currently being studied, and the gaps that remain. Doing this well is not a matter of description. It is not just an account of who said what, when.

The objective is to critique the discourse: to analyse, evaluate and synthesise it so that the value of your own research becomes clear. Analysis breaks the discourse into its themes and positions. Evaluation weighs how strong and well-supported each one is. Synthesis draws them together into a picture no single source gave you. The gap you identify is the opening your research will fill.

title: Explore the concept
body: A literature review is built to establish four things about the discourse. Read each card to see the work it does.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Key works and authors
_items.subtitle: The map
_items.text: A review sets out the works and voices that matter in the area, so a reader can see the territory your research sits in and who has shaped it.

_items.title: Themes and debates
_items.subtitle: The argument
_items.text: It draws out the recurring themes and the live debates, including the controversial points, rather than treating each source as a separate fact to report.

_items.title: What is studied now
_items.subtitle: The present
_items.text: It shows which questions the field is currently working on, placing your project in a conversation that is still moving, not a settled past.

_items.title: The gaps
_items.subtitle: The opening
_items.text: It identifies what is missing or unresolved. The gap is the point of the review: it is the opening your own research is set up to fill.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students write the opening of a literature review on the same topic, using the same handful of sources.

{{learner-a}} writes a sentence per source: one author found X, another reported Y, a third argued Z. Each source is summarised accurately and in turn. But the paragraph only lists them. Nothing is weighed, nothing is connected, and the reader cannot tell what the student makes of the field or where their own research would sit. This is description.

{{learner-b}} groups the same sources by theme, notes where they agree and where they clash, and weighs which findings are better supported. The paragraph then draws them together into a claim none of them made alone, and points to a question none has answered. This is a review: it analyses, evaluates and synthesises, and the gap it names is where the student's research begins.

Both students read the same sources. Only {{learner-b}} critiqued the discourse rather than reporting it.

title: Practical guidance
body: These habits turn a list of sources into a review. Try them on your next piece of reading.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I grouped the sources by theme or position, rather than taking them one at a time?
Have I said where sources agree and where they disagree?
Have I weighed which findings are better supported, not just reported them?
Have I drawn the sources together into a point none of them made alone?
Have I named a gap or unresolved question in the discourse?
Have I made clear how my own research answers to that gap?

title: Formative check: what a review does
displayTitle: Which of these best describes what a literature review is meant to do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option best describes what a literature review is meant to do?

_items.text: Critique the discourse, analysing, evaluating and synthesising it to show where your research fits.
_items.feedback: Yes. A review critiques the discourse rather than reporting it.

_items.text: Describe each relevant source in turn, reporting accurately what each one says.
_items.feedback: Accurate description of each source in turn is a list, not a review.

_items.text: List as many relevant sources as possible to show the breadth of your reading.
_items.feedback: Breadth of reading is not the point; what you do with the sources is.

_items.text: Summarise the single most authoritative source in the field in full.
_items.feedback: A review works across the discourse, not through one source alone.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A literature review critiques the discourse by analysing, evaluating and synthesising it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that works WITH the sources, rather than listing or summarising them.
_incorrect.final: A review critiques the discourse: it analyses, evaluates and synthesises. Describing each source, listing many, or summarising one are not reviewing.

title: Formative check: recognising the moves
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's paragraph a review rather than a description?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's paragraph a review rather than a description?

_items.text: It grouped and weighed the sources and drew them into a point none made alone.
_items.feedback: Yes. Grouping, weighing and synthesising is reviewing, not describing.

_items.text: It summarised each source more accurately than the first student.
_items.feedback: Accurate summary is still description, however careful.

_items.text: It discussed more sources than the first student's paragraph.
_items.feedback: The number of sources is not what makes a paragraph a review.

_items.text: It quoted the authors' own words rather than paraphrasing them.
_items.feedback: Quoting rather than paraphrasing does not turn a list into a review.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second paragraph grouped, weighed and synthesised the sources, which is reviewing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID with the sources, beyond summarising them.
_incorrect.final: The paragraph was a review because it grouped and weighed the sources and synthesised them into a new point. More sources, closer summary or direct quotation are still description.

title: Formative check: reviewing versus listing
displayTitle: You are reviewing the literature for a project in {{context}}. Which sentence reviews the literature rather than merely listing it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which sentence reviews the literature rather than merely listing it?

_items.text: Taken together these studies point one way, but the better-controlled ones are more cautious, leaving the question open.
_items.feedback: Yes. That weighs and synthesises the studies, which is reviewing them in {{context}}.

_items.text: Smith (2019) found one result; Jones (2020) found another; Patel (2021) found a third.
_items.feedback: Listing findings one after another is description, not a review.

_items.text: This topic has been written about a great deal in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Noting that work exists does not review any of it.

_items.text: The most cited paper in {{context}} reports the following findings.
_items.feedback: Reporting one paper's findings is not a review of the discourse.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing the studies against each other and drawing out an open question reviews the literature in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the sentence that weighs and connects the studies, rather than listing or reporting them.
_incorrect.final: The reviewing sentence weighs the studies against each other and synthesises an open question. Listing findings, noting that work exists, or reporting one paper are all description.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a literature review you have read or written in your subject. Did it critique the discourse, or did it mostly list sources one by one? What is one move you could make to turn a list into a review?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A literature review critiques the discourse rather than describing it. It establishes the key works, themes, debates and gaps, and uses analysis, evaluation and synthesis to show where your research fits. You can now tell a review from a list, recognise those moves in a worked example, and spot a sentence that reviews rather than reports. The next lesson turns to the proposal that such a review supports.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 157 to 160 of Chapter 9, 'Writing for Assessment', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: A research proposal is where a project is first set out for someone else to judge. It is tempting to treat it as a statement of a topic: here is the area I want to work on. A strong proposal does more. It is a framework of questions, carefully built to narrow that area into a project that can actually be done, and to show why it is worth doing.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You know how a research project is shaped in outline. Here you produce the document that commits to it: a proposal whose questions move from a broad topic to a specific, researchable focus, and which shows the freshness of that focus rather than claiming total originality.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how a proposal's questions build a framework for the whole project
recognise how a worked proposal moves from a general topic to a specific, fresh focus
choose the question that sharpens a broad topic into a researchable one in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A research proposal is often built as a series of questions, created to make you engage with the topic and its discourse at a deeper level, but in a guided and structured way. Answering each question as fully as you can builds a framework for the whole project: what you will study, why it matters, what is already known, how you will approach it, and what you expect it to add.

The work of a proposal is to narrow. A general topic becomes a specific, answerable focus as the questions sharpen it. And the test it must pass is not originality in the sense of something entirely new, which little research can honestly claim. It is freshness: a perspective, a case or a combination that has not been looked at in quite this way before.

title: Explore the concept
body: A proposal is built from questions, and each one does a distinct job in the framework. Open each to see what it settles.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: What am I studying?
_items.body: The first questions fix the topic and turn it into something specific. A broad area becomes a focused question the project can actually answer, rather than a subject it could only gesture at.

_items.title: Why does it matter?
_items.body: The proposal must say why the question is worth asking: what is at stake, who the answer would matter to, and what the field gains. This is where freshness is argued, not originality for its own sake.

_items.title: What is already known?
_items.body: A proposal places the project in the existing discourse, drawing on the literature review to show what has been established and, as importantly, what has not. The gap is what the project is for.

_items.title: How will I approach it?
_items.body: Finally the proposal sets out method and scope: how the question will be investigated, with what, and within what limits. A fresh focus with no workable method is not yet a project.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students draft a proposal starting from the same broad interest.

{{learner-a}} writes that the project will study the broad topic, because it is important and under-researched, and will read widely before deciding what to do. The topic is named, but nothing is narrowed. The proposal gives no specific question, no sense of what is already known, and no method. A reader cannot tell what would actually be done, or why this project rather than any other.

{{learner-b}} starts from the same interest but drives it through questions. The broad topic becomes one specific case; a reason is given for why that case matters now; the existing work is summarised to show the gap; and a workable method is set against it. The focus is not wholly new, but it is fresh: this case, approached in this way, has not been looked at before.

Both began with the same interest. Only {{learner-b}} built a framework of questions that turned it into a project.

title: Practical guidance
body: These moves turn a broad interest into a workable proposal. Try them on a topic of your own.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I turned my broad topic into one specific, answerable question?
Have I said why the question matters, and to whom?
Have I used the literature to show what is already known and what is not?
Have I named the gap my project will fill?
Have I set out a method that could actually answer the question?
Have I shown the freshness of the focus, rather than claiming it is wholly original?

title: Formative check: the framework of questions
displayTitle: Why is a research proposal best thought of as a framework of questions?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is a research proposal best thought of as a framework of questions?

_items.text: Because answering each question in turn settles what, why, what is known and how, for the whole project.
_items.feedback: Yes. The questions build the framework the project runs on.

_items.text: Because a long list of questions shows the marker how much the student has read.
_items.feedback: The point is not quantity; it is what the questions settle.

_items.text: Because questions are easier to write than a continuous argument.
_items.feedback: Ease of writing is not why a proposal is built from questions.

_items.text: Because the proposal is mainly a test of whether the topic is original.
_items.feedback: A proposal tests freshness and feasibility, not total originality.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Answering the questions in turn settles the project's what, why, what-is-known and how.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the questions, taken together, actually build.
_incorrect.final: The questions matter because answering them builds the framework: what you study, why, what is known, and how. It is not about quantity, ease, or originality alone.

title: Formative check: general to specific
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that turned a broad interest into a project?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What turned the second student's broad interest into a project?

_items.text: Drove the topic through questions into a specific, fresh focus with a workable method.
_items.feedback: Yes. Narrowing to a fresh, workable focus is what makes a project.

_items.text: Promised to read widely before deciding what to do.
_items.feedback: Promising to read widely leaves the topic unnarrowed.

_items.text: Chose a topic that was entirely original and had never been studied.
_items.feedback: Total originality is not what a proposal needs; freshness is.

_items.text: Named the broad topic and explained that it was important.
_items.feedback: Naming a broad topic and calling it important is not yet a project.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student narrowed the topic through questions into a fresh, workable focus.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID to the topic, beyond naming it or promising to read.
_incorrect.final: The second student drove the topic through questions into a specific, fresh focus with a method. Reading widely, claiming originality or naming the topic do not make a project.

title: Formative check: sharpening a topic
displayTitle: You are narrowing a broad topic in {{context}} into a proposal. Which question best sharpens it into a researchable focus?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which question best sharpens a broad topic into a researchable focus?

_items.text: Which specific case, group or setting in {{context}} will I study, and over what period?
_items.feedback: Yes. That question narrows the topic to something you can actually investigate in {{context}}.

_items.text: Why is this broad area of {{context}} important to so many people?
_items.feedback: Importance matters, but this question does not narrow the topic.

_items.text: How much has already been written about {{context}} in general?
_items.feedback: Volume of existing writing does not sharpen your focus.

_items.text: Is there any topic in {{context}} that is completely original?
_items.feedback: Chasing total originality is the wrong test; freshness and focus are what you need.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Asking which specific case, group or setting narrows a broad topic into a researchable focus in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the question that narrows the topic to something you could actually study.
_incorrect.final: The sharpening question fixes a specific case, group or setting and a period. Asking why it matters, how much exists, or whether it is wholly original does not narrow the focus.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a topic you might research in your subject. What is one question that would narrow it from a broad area into a specific, researchable focus? What would make that focus fresh?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A research proposal is a framework of questions that narrows a broad topic into a specific, answerable focus and shows its freshness rather than claiming total originality. You can now explain how the questions build the framework, recognise the move from general to specific in a worked proposal, and choose the question that sharpens a topic. The final lesson turns to the report that presents completed research.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 150 to 157 of Chapter 9, 'Writing for Assessment', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: When research is done, a report presents it. In the sciences especially, the report follows a settled structure, close to that of a research article. The structure is not a formality. Each section answers a particular question for the reader, and putting the right material in the right section is much of what makes a report clear.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You can read a report and follow its parts. Here you produce one: organising your work into the core elements a reader expects and, above all, keeping what you found separate from what you think it means.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use the core elements of a report (introduction, methodology, results and discussion) for their proper purpose
tell results apart from discussion in a worked report
match a passage to the report section it belongs in, in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A report is structured along settled lines. At its core are four elements. The introduction sets out the question and why it matters. The methodology says exactly what was done, so that another researcher could repeat it. The results report what was found, plainly and without interpretation. The discussion then interprets those findings, saying what they mean and how far they can be trusted. Depending on the discipline, a report may add a title, abstract, conclusion and reference list around this core.

The distinction that most often goes wrong is between results and discussion. Results are the findings themselves: what the data showed. Discussion is what you make of them: their meaning, their limits, their place in the wider field. Keeping the two apart lets a reader see the evidence first, and then your reading of it, rather than the two tangled together.

title: Explore the concept
body: A report moves through its sections in order, each answering one question for the reader.
instruction: Step through each section to see the work it does.

_items.title: Introduction
_items.body: Sets out the question the report addresses and why it matters, and places it against what is already known.

_items.title: Methodology
_items.body: States exactly what was done and how, in enough detail that another researcher could repeat the work and get comparable results.

_items.title: Results
_items.body: Reports what was found, plainly and in order. This section presents the evidence; it does not yet interpret it.

_items.title: Discussion
_items.body: Interprets the findings: what they mean, how far they can be trusted, their limits, and how they sit in the wider field.

_items.title: Conclusion
_items.body: Draws the answer together, states what the work adds, and points to what should follow. Around this core sit the title, abstract and references.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students write up the same small study and reach the results section.

{{learner-a}} writes that the scores were higher in the second group, which shows the method clearly works and should be adopted widely. The finding is there, but it is tangled with interpretation and a recommendation. A reader cannot see the plain evidence on its own, and claims about what it means have arrived before the discussion, where they could be weighed.

{{learner-b}} writes, in the results, that the second group scored higher by a stated margin, and saves the reading of that difference for the discussion. There, {{learner-b}} asks whether the margin is large enough to matter, notes that the sample was small, and holds back from recommending anything until the evidence can bear it. Evidence first, interpretation second.

Both found the same result. Only {{learner-b}} kept the results and the discussion in their proper sections.

title: Practical guidance
body: Use these checks to keep each part of a report doing its own job.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Does my introduction give the question and why it matters, not the findings?
Could another researcher repeat the work from my methodology alone?
Do my results report only what was found, with no interpretation?
Have I saved what the findings mean for the discussion?
Does my discussion weigh the findings, including their limits?
Is each piece of material in the one section where a reader expects it?

title: Formative check: the core elements
displayTitle: Which section of a report states exactly what was done, so that another researcher could repeat it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which section states exactly what was done, so another researcher could repeat it?

_items.text: The methodology.
_items.feedback: Yes. The methodology makes the work repeatable.

_items.text: The introduction.
_items.feedback: The introduction frames the question; it does not detail what was done.

_items.text: The results.
_items.feedback: The results report what was found, not how it was done.

_items.text: The discussion.
_items.feedback: The discussion interprets the findings; it does not record the method.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The methodology states exactly what was done, so the work can be repeated.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which section lets another researcher repeat the work?
_incorrect.final: The methodology states what was done, in enough detail to repeat. The introduction frames, the results report, and the discussion interprets.

title: Formative check: results versus discussion
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that the first did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do that the first did not?

_items.text: Reported the finding plainly in the results and saved its interpretation for the discussion.
_items.feedback: Yes. Keeping evidence and interpretation in separate sections is the point.

_items.text: Found a larger difference between the two groups.
_items.feedback: Both found the same result; the difference was in how they wrote it up.

_items.text: Recommended the method more strongly than the first student.
_items.feedback: The second student held back from recommending, rather than pushing harder.

_items.text: Wrote a longer results section than the first student.
_items.feedback: Length is not what distinguished the two write-ups.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student kept the plain finding in the results and its interpretation in the discussion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at WHERE each student put the finding and its interpretation.
_incorrect.final: The second student reported the finding in the results and saved interpretation for the discussion. A bigger difference, a stronger recommendation or more length were not the point.

title: Formative check: placing a passage
displayTitle: You are drafting a report in {{context}}. A sentence weighs what a finding means and notes its limits. Which section does it belong in?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A sentence weighs what a finding means and notes its limits. Which section is it?

_items.text: The discussion.
_items.feedback: Yes. Weighing meaning and limits is the work of the discussion in {{context}}.

_items.text: The results.
_items.feedback: The results report the finding plainly; weighing it comes later.

_items.text: The methodology.
_items.feedback: The methodology says what was done, not what the findings mean.

_items.text: The introduction.
_items.feedback: The introduction frames the question; it does not interpret findings.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing what a finding means and noting its limits belongs in the discussion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which section interprets findings, rather than reporting or framing them?
_incorrect.final: A sentence that weighs meaning and notes limits belongs in the discussion. The results report, the methodology records the method, and the introduction frames the question.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a report you have written or read in your subject. Was the line between results and discussion clear, or did interpretation creep into the results? What is one thing you could do to keep them apart?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A report is structured so that each core element does one job: the introduction frames the question, the methodology makes the work repeatable, the results present the evidence, and the discussion interprets it. You can now use these elements for their proper purpose, tell results apart from discussion, and place a passage in the section where it belongs. With the review, the proposal and the report, you have the three genres that carry research.

title: Assessment introduction
body:
This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Now that you have finished, rate your confidence again. Comparing the two shows how far you have moved.

_patterns.rose: Your confidence in {{item}} has grown over the course.
_patterns.stayedHigh: You were confident about {{item}} and remain so.
_patterns.stayedLow: {{item}} still feels uncertain. It would be worth revisiting this before you move on.
_patterns.noMovement: Your confidence in {{item}} has not shifted much.
_patterns.dropped: Your confidence in {{item}} has fallen. This often reflects a more accurate view of what is involved rather than a step backwards, and noticing it is itself progress. It would be worth another look.

_summary._predominantlyUp: Your confidence grew across most of these.
_summary._mixed: Your confidence grew in some areas and settled lower in others. Both are useful to know.
_summary._flatOrLow: Several of these still feel unsettled, which is worth knowing now.

_feedback._standalone: Here is where your confidence sits on each statement.

_forward._summative: The check ahead is where this confidence will be tested.
_forward._application: The real measure will be how this holds up when you next apply it in your own work.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. The three documents that carry research are no longer just genres you read, but genres you can produce. You can write a literature review that critiques the discourse rather than listing sources. You can shape a proposal as a framework of questions that narrows a topic and shows its freshness. And you can structure a report so its core elements each do their work, with results and discussion kept apart. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, these genres are the working documents of your research. A dissertation opens with a literature review; a funded project begins as a proposal; findings are communicated as a report. Each time you write one to its purpose, rather than merely to its format, you are doing the work that research degrees and research careers are built on.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced Researching and Research Methods course takes you into running research with rigour and ethics, from consent and data handling to the principles of research integrity. Going wider: Academic Writing and Criticality sharpen the writing and judgement that every one of these genres depends on.

body: What is the main job of a literature review?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the main job of a literature review?

_items.text: To critique the discourse, analysing, evaluating and synthesising it to show where your research fits.
_items.feedback: Yes. A review critiques the discourse.

_items.text: To describe each relevant source in turn, reporting what each one says.
_items.feedback: That is a list, not a review.

_items.text: To list as many relevant sources as possible.
_items.feedback: Breadth of citation is not reviewing.

_items.text: To summarise the single most authoritative source in full.
_items.feedback: A review works across the discourse, not one source.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A literature review critiques the discourse rather than describing it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a review does beyond reporting sources.

body: Which sentence belongs in a literature review rather than a simple list of sources?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which sentence reviews rather than lists?

_items.text: Taken together the stronger studies point one way, leaving one question open.
_items.feedback: Yes. That weighs and synthesises the studies.

_items.text: Author A found X; Author B found Y; Author C found Z.
_items.feedback: Listing findings one by one is description.

_items.text: This topic has been researched a great deal.
_items.feedback: Noting that work exists does not review it.

_items.text: The following sources were read for this project.
_items.feedback: A reading list is not a review.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing and synthesising the studies is reviewing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the sentence that weighs and connects the studies.

body: A research proposal is best understood as...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A research proposal is best understood as...

_items.text: a framework of questions that narrows a topic and shows its freshness.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is what a proposal is.

_items.text: a statement of a broad topic the student finds important.
_items.feedback: A named topic is not yet a proposal.

_items.text: a promise to read widely before deciding what to do.
_items.feedback: That leaves the topic unnarrowed.

_items.text: a claim that the topic is entirely original.
_items.feedback: Freshness, not total originality, is the test.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A proposal is a framework of questions that narrows a topic and shows its freshness.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the proposal's questions build.

body: What does 'freshness' mean in a research proposal?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does freshness mean in a proposal?

_items.text: A perspective, case or combination not looked at in quite this way before.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is freshness.

_items.text: A topic that is completely new and has never been studied.
_items.feedback: That is total originality, which little research can claim.

_items.text: A topic that is currently popular in the field.
_items.feedback: Popularity is not freshness.

_items.text: A longer reading list than other proposals.
_items.feedback: Freshness is about perspective, not quantity.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Freshness is a perspective or case not looked at in quite this way before.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Freshness is not the same as total originality.

body: Which report section reports what was found, without interpreting it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which section reports findings without interpreting them?

_items.text: The results.
_items.feedback: Yes. The results present the evidence plainly.

_items.text: The discussion.
_items.feedback: The discussion interprets the findings.

_items.text: The introduction.
_items.feedback: The introduction frames the question.

_items.text: The methodology.
_items.feedback: The methodology records what was done.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The results report what was found, without interpretation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which section presents the plain evidence?

body: A sentence that interprets findings and notes their limits belongs in which section?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A sentence interpreting findings and noting limits belongs where?

_items.text: The discussion.
_items.feedback: Yes. Interpreting and weighing findings is the discussion's work.

_items.text: The results.
_items.feedback: The results report findings; they do not interpret them.

_items.text: The methodology.
_items.feedback: The methodology records the method, not the meaning.

_items.text: The introduction.
_items.feedback: The introduction frames the question, not the findings.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Interpreting findings and noting their limits belongs in the discussion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which section weighs what the findings mean?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: how a literature review critiques the discourse, how a proposal is built as a framework of questions, and how a report structures its core elements. On their own they are three separate genres. This lesson brings them together into one connected research project.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run a full research project end to end. The aim is to see the three genres as one connected whole rather than three separate tasks, so the link carries into the research your degree will ask of you.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect what a review, a proposal and a report each do into one research project
analyse how the three genres work as one project in a worked research example
apply the three genres together to shape a piece of research in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body: A research project is one connected whole, carried by three documents in turn. The literature review maps the discourse and names a gap. The proposal turns that gap into a framework of questions and a workable plan. The report then presents what the plan produced, keeping results apart from discussion. Each genre carries the work of the one before it forward.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, the three genres pass one thread between them. The gap your review finds becomes the question your proposal asks. The plan your proposal sets becomes the method your report describes. Written this way, the three documents read as one project rather than three loose exercises.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a research project you might take on in your subject. What gap would your review look for, and how would that gap shape your proposal's question and your report? There are no right or wrong answers.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A research project is strongest when the review, the proposal and the report work as one connected whole. You can now bring the three genres together, recognise them working as one project, and plan how they will connect in your own research. It is the thread running through all three, not any single document, that makes a project hold together.

title: The steps as one process
body: A research project runs as one connected sequence, each stage carrying the work of the one before it forward. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Review
_items.body: Review the literature to map the discourse and name the gap your project will address.

_items.title: Propose
_items.body: Shape a proposal that turns the gap into a research question and a workable plan.

_items.title: Carry out
_items.body: Carry out the work the proposal set out, gathering what you need to answer the question.

_items.title: Report
_items.body: Write the report to present the findings, keeping results apart from discussion.

title: Worked example
body: Two students work on projects of similar size. One treats the review, the proposal and the report as three separate tasks, so the report answers a question the proposal never set. The other lets each genre feed the next: the review's gap shapes the proposal's question, and the report answers that same question. The second project holds together, because the three genres worked as one.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to connect the three genres
body: Use these questions to keep the review, the proposal and the report working as one project.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Does my literature review end by naming a clear gap?
Does my proposal turn that gap into a specific, answerable question?
Does my method follow from the question my proposal set?
Do my results report what I found, with interpretation saved for the discussion?
Can a reader trace one thread from the review through to the report?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat the review, the proposal and the report as one connected project rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it better to treat the review, the proposal and the report as one connected project rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it better to treat the review, the proposal and the report as one connected project rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because each genre carries the one before it forward: the review's gap becomes the proposal's question, and the proposal's plan shapes the report.
_items.feedback: Yes. Each genre carries the one before it forward, so the project holds together.

_items.text: Because writing three documents in a fixed order saves time whatever the project is about.
_items.feedback: The order is not about saving time; it is about one genre feeding the next.

_items.text: Because a marker only cares that all three documents are present, not how they connect.
_items.feedback: A marker reads for the thread between them, not just that all three exist.

_items.text: Because the three genres use the same format, so one template fits all of them.
_items.feedback: The genres differ in form; what connects them is the thread of the project.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three genres form one connected arc: a gap found, a plan made, and the findings reported.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the gap, the question and the plan pass from one genre to the next.

displayTitle: A student finds a gap in the literature, builds a proposal whose question targets that gap, carries out the study, and writes a report whose results answer the same question. What does this show?
body: A student finds a gap in the literature, builds a proposal whose question targets that gap, carries out the study, and writes a report whose results answer the same question. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student finds a gap in the literature, builds a proposal whose question targets that gap, carries out the study, and writes a report whose results answer the same question. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three genres worked as one connected project, each carrying the work of the one before it forward.
_items.feedback: Yes. One thread runs from the review's gap to the report's findings.

_items.text: That the student wrote more words than a project of this kind needs.
_items.feedback: Length is not the point; the connection between the genres is.

_items.text: That the literature review alone decided the whole project's success.
_items.feedback: The review started the thread, but the proposal and report carried it on.

_items.text: That the report could have been written before the proposal with no difference.
_items.feedback: The order matters: the report answers the question the proposal set.

_feedback.correct: That's right. One thread runs from the review's gap, through the proposal's question, to the report's findings.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the same question is carried from the review all the way to the report.

displayTitle: You want to plan a piece of research in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats the review, the proposal and the report as one connected project?
body: You want to plan a piece of research in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats the review, the proposal and the report as one connected project?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to plan a piece of research in your subject this term. Which plan best treats the review, the proposal and the report as one connected project?

_items.text: Let the review's gap set the proposal's question, let that question shape the method, and let the report answer the same question.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, one question runs from the gap you find to the findings you report.

_items.text: Write the three documents separately, on unrelated topics, so each one stands alone.
_items.feedback: Three unrelated documents are not one project; the thread is lost.

_items.text: Start with the report, then write a proposal and a review to fit the findings afterwards.
_items.feedback: Writing the report first leaves the review and proposal with nothing to shape.

_items.text: Pick whichever genre is easiest and leave the other two for another module.
_items.feedback: Leaving two genres out breaks the project into loose pieces.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, one question runs from the gap you find to the findings you report.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The connected plan carries one question from the review through to the report.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What best describes the link between the literature review, the research proposal and the report?
body: What best describes the link between the literature review, the research proposal and the report?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What best describes the link between the literature review, the research proposal and the report?

_items.text: They form one connected project: the review finds a gap, the proposal turns it into a question and plan, and the report presents the findings.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: They are three unrelated documents that happen to share a reading list.
_items.feedback: They share a thread, not just a reading list.

_items.text: They are three names for the same document written at different times.
_items.feedback: They are distinct genres, each doing a different job.

_items.text: They must each be written on a different topic to avoid repetition.
_items.feedback: They work on one project, not three different topics.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A researcher's report presents results that answer the exact question their proposal set, and that question grew from a gap their review named. What does this show?
body: A researcher's report presents results that answer the exact question their proposal set, and that question grew from a gap their review named. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A researcher's report presents results that answer the exact question their proposal set, and that question grew from a gap their review named. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three genres worked as one connected project, each carrying the work of the one before it forward.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: That the researcher wrote the three documents in the wrong order.
_items.feedback: The order here is right: review, then proposal, then report.

_items.text: That the literature review was unnecessary once the report was written.
_items.feedback: The review named the gap the whole project answers.

_items.text: That the results and discussion should be merged into one section.
_items.feedback: Results and discussion stay apart; that is not what this shows.
